name: Nikhil Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union or party, and nothing you say gets your name on it. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. My union rep told me you lot were independent, otherwise I wouldn't have come. I'm not a talker, so you'll have to pull it out of me a bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Fair enough. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at half five, I'm on the Meadow Park estate by seven, that's a new build of a hundred and forty houses for one of the big developers. I'm a carpenter's mate, so I carry the timber, cut what Steve marks for me, hang the odd door, sweep up after the first-fix lads. I'm forty-three and still the one who gets sent for the pallet of joist hangers, because I only came to the trade three years ago when the biscuit factory shut. I like the smell of fresh pine and the end of the day when a roof's on. What wears me out is my knees, and the site boss chasing us for numbers because the developer's chasing him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Half the lads on site have been going on about robots for two years and here we are, still carrying plasterboard up the stairs by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my head down and keep earning, which is all I want. But I'm not stupid, the developer would still be squeezing us whether there's AI or not. Hype or no hype, the people at the top don't share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Steve, try to get my card upgraded so I'm on the skilled rate, and keep paying my union subs. I'd maybe ask about the evening course at the college again, but it's Tuesday nights and that's Farah's late shift at the school, so probably not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Though there's always a bit of a knot in my stomach, because I've been told things were safe before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the biscuit factory. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eighteen years on the packing line at Harlow's, and then they put in the new wrapping machines and the line went from twelve of us to three. I was one of the nine. They gave us a month's pay and a leaflet about retraining, and the leaflet had a website on it, which is no use to a man who doesn't do websites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stay like this, what does money look like for your family over the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight, same as now. We've got about two weeks of money in the account at any time, and the mortgage on the house on Clement Road eats most of it. If the boiler goes, it goes on the credit card, and that's that.

S0.say: Told you so, all that robot talk was overblown. We're all still carrying plasterboard up the stairs by hand, same as ever.
S0.think: It means I keep my head down and keep earning, which is all I want. But the developer would squeeze us with or without AI, and I've been told I was safe before.
S0.do: Carries on as Steve's carpenter's mate and tries to get his skills card upgraded to the skilled pay rate. Keeps paying union subs and probably skips the Tuesday evening college course because it clashes with his wife's shift.
S0.feel: Mostly relieved, with a knot of worry left over from being told before that his job was safe.
S0.quote: They gave us a month's pay and a leaflet about retraining, and the leaflet had a website on it, which is no use to a man who doesn't do websites.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the calmest picture he can't fully relax, because he has already lost one job to machines. His money is so thin that a boiler repair goes on credit. He blames the people at the top rather than the technology itself, which shapes everything that follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get stuck in now, before it's too late. I'd be the one at the canteen table saying we should be negotiating what machines come on site and who gets kept on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm the first one out. I'm the carrier and the cutter, and that's the stuff a machine does first. A skilled carpenter who can read a drawing and fix a mistake, maybe they keep him. Me, I'm the easy saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting, which I don't do now. I'd cancel the kids' after-school football club, that's 40 a month, and stop the takeaway on Fridays. I wouldn't go near the AI stuff myself, I wouldn't know where to start and I don't want to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm back at Harlow's watching them unload the new machines off the lorry. You know what's coming, you just don't know which week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, the old labourer I have lunch with in the van. He's sixty-one, no pension worth talking about, and he can't read well. If they bring in a machine that lifts the boards, Ray's gone, and nobody's going to retrain Ray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Farah the night you heard about the first job cuts on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not yet, love, but get ready. Then I'd probably sit in the car outside for ten minutes before going in, so the kids don't see my face. That's what I did last time.

S1.say: The union needs to get stuck in now, before it's too late. We should be negotiating which machines come on site and who gets kept on.
S1.think: I'm the first one out, because carrying and cutting is the stuff a machine does first. They might keep a skilled carpenter, but I'm the easy saving.
S1.do: Starts going to every union branch meeting and cuts the kids' 40-a-month football club and the Friday takeaway. Refuses to try AI tools himself because he doesn't know where to start and doesn't want to.
S1.feel: Dread that feels like the factory closing all over again, waiting to find out which week it lands.
S1.quote: If they bring in a machine that lifts the boards, Ray's gone, and nobody's going to retrain Ray.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is about fighting together, while privately he has already written himself off. The worry for Ray, his lunch mate, came quicker than worry for himself. The detail of sitting in the car so the kids don't see his face is a memory, not a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this should be stopped, or at least the government should make the companies pay for it. If a robot does my job, the company that owns it should be paying for my kids' dinners, that's what I'd put on Facebook, if I posted things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's over for people like me. I'm forty-three, I didn't finish school, and there's no other building work round here to run to. In two years I'd be on benefits with a mortgage and two kids, and I don't see what else happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to the union office on Station Street and ask what they're doing, and sign every petition going. I'd phone my brother Arif about whether we could move in with him if it came to it, and I'd go to the council about help with the mortgage. We'd cut everything, the phones, the car insurance down to the minimum, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't sleep well now, and in that picture I don't think I'd sleep at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two years. What does having only two years change for you, compared with a slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. It's not even enough to finish a college course, if I could afford one, which I can't. With the slow one I could at least hope to hang on till something changed, but with two years there's nothing to hang on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card first, then the water bill, and the mortgage last, because you don't play games with the roof over your kids. I've seen a neighbour lose a house. The bailiff's van parked outside for an hour and everyone pretending not to look.

S2.say: This should be stopped, or the companies should be made to pay for it. If a robot does my job, the company that owns it should be paying for my kids' dinners.
S2.think: It's over for people like me: forty-three, didn't finish school, and no other building work round here. In two years I'd be on benefits with a mortgage and two kids.
S2.do: Goes to the union office on Station Street, signs every petition and asks the council about mortgage help. Phones his brother Arif about moving in together and cuts phones, car insurance and everything else to the bone.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone from under him; he already sleeps badly and thinks he wouldn't sleep at all.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. It's not even enough to finish a college course, if I could afford one, which I can't.
S2.fieldNote: This is where he runs out of options: no savings, no local alternatives and no wish to learn new technology. His plan is all about leaning on others, the union, the council and his brother. The bailiff's van story shows how close losing the house already feels to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, only louder. I'd say we've got five years to make the rules, so let's make them, and I'd go on the march if the union called one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years buys me a bit, but I'm not the type to reinvent myself. I took the building job because it was the only one going, and it took me three years to get half decent. I don't have another one of those in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put fifty a month away, even if it means no holiday at all. I'd go to the branch every month and help with the leaflets, and I'd vote for whoever promised to tax the robot owners. Once it arrives I'd be at the job centre, same as everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less like a cliff and more like a hill I'm walking down and I can see the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do in the years before it arrives, while you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Farah to look into the schools, so the kids learn the stuff I can't. And I'd put a bit by every month, and I'd help the union build a list of who's on which site, so when it comes we're organised, not scattered. That's the bit I can do with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch the AI tools. Would five years change your mind on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My daughter Zara does my timesheet on the app because I always press the wrong thing. I know that sounds stubborn, but I'd rather spend the time fighting for a fair deal than learning a gadget that's coming for me anyway.

S3.say: We've got five years to make the rules, so let's make them. If the union calls a march, I'll be on it.
S3.think: Five years buys me a bit, but I'm not the type to reinvent myself. It took me three years to get half decent at this, and I don't have another one of those in me.
S3.do: Tries to save 50 a month by giving up holidays and helps the union with leaflets and a list of who works on which site. Votes for whoever would tax robot owners and expects to go to the job centre once it arrives.
S3.feel: Heavy, like walking down a hill he can see the bottom of, rather than falling off a cliff.
S3.quote: Less like a cliff and more like a hill I'm walking down and I can see the bottom.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't make him more adaptable, it makes him more organised. He would spend the five years getting the union ready and pushing his kids towards new skills rather than learning any himself. He was open about choosing not to learn the technology, and gave his reason plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, a fair deal for workers, training paid for by the companies, that sort of thing. I'd say it at the branch, and I'd say it to the councillor when she comes knocking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is a lot more breathing room. If nothing else, I'd get close to paying off the credit card and the kids would be nearly grown. But I'd still be the bloke on the edge of a site who can't do much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on Meadow Park and the next estate after it as long as they'll have me. I'd keep up the union work and put a little by each month, and I'd stand for branch secretary if nobody else will. When it comes I'd want to be in the room when they decide who gets paid off and how much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frantic. I could plan for ten years, and I like a plan, even if it ends somewhere I don't want to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fifty-three by 2036. Does ten years feel different from five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. In ten years Zara's at college or working and Imran's finishing school, so it's not little kids going hungry. At fifty-three nobody's hiring me for anything, so I'd want to get to that point with no debt at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Imran and Zara about their own futures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them don't do what I did, taking whatever job is going and hoping it lasts. Find out what the machines can't do and do that, and join the union the day you start.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do it properly. That means a fair deal for workers and training paid for by the companies, not by us.
S4.think: Ten years is a lot more breathing room, enough to clear the credit card and see the kids nearly grown. But I'd still be the bloke on the edge of a site who can't do much else.
S4.do: Keeps working on Meadow Park and the next estate for as long as he's wanted, and keeps saving a little each month. Steps up in the union, possibly as branch secretary, so he has a say in redundancy terms when the time comes.
S4.feel: Worried but not frantic, and steadied by having time to make a plan, even one that ends badly.
S4.quote: Find out what the machines can't do and do that, and join the union the day you start.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture moves him from panic to steady worry, mostly because his kids would be older and his debts smaller. He still does not picture himself changing trade. The advice to his children puts his hopes in the next generation and in collective strength.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because there's no time to do anything and no money to do it with. What would help is the companies being made to pay into something for the people they replace, a proper wage while you find your feet, not a leaflet with a website on it. And the union being in the room from the start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Everyone talks about AI like it's the weather, like it just happens to us. It doesn't, somebody signs the order for the machine, and I'd like to know their name.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI like it's the weather, like it just happens to us. It doesn't, somebody signs the order for the machine, and I'd like to know their name.
portrait: Nikhil is a 43-year-old carpenter's mate on a new housing estate, who came to building three years ago after machines cut his biscuit factory job. With about two weeks of money in the bank, a mortgage and two school-age kids, he has no room for a bad month. He avoids new technology, lets his daughter fill in his timesheet app and puts his faith in the union instead. He is uneasy even in the calm picture, panicked by the two-year AGI picture, and steadier only when ten years gives his kids time to grow up. Throughout, he blames the people who sign off on the machines, not the machines themselves.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to prepare and no money to prepare with.
whatWouldHelp: Companies paying into a fund that gives replaced workers a proper wage while they find their feet, and the union being involved in decisions from the start.
